case_study_insert.main_stem: Verdant Insulation Materials (VIML) is a private limited company in the eco-friendly construction materials sector, employing a workforce of 28. Founded in 2013 by Aisha Rahman, the business supplies recycled-fibre insulation to builders and operates a hierarchical structure with democratic leadership. VIML plans to invest $450,000 in a recycled-fibre insulation line, financed by $180,000 of hire purchase and $270,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $240,000 a year, a variable cost of $9.00 a unit and a selling price of $15.00, and currently produces 80,000 units a year. VIML faces two problems: a skills gap in machine operation and rising production waste; trial rolls recently recorded a 2.7% defect rate.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Market Research Summary — Q3 2025: A survey of 300 builders found 66% would switch to recycled-fibre insulation if the price was within $0.30 of standard rolls, and 58% said supplier carbon data influences their purchase. Trial sales reached 16,000 rolls at a defect rate of 2.7%, down from 4.4% a year earlier. Complaints about settling fell from 26 to 12 a month. Delivery lead time is 4.1 days. Production waste is 5.5% of input. A training audit shows 11 of 28 staff have not completed on-the-job training on the new fibre line; off-the-job courses at the college cost $540 per employee.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Profit or Loss and Capital employed data of Verdant Insulation Materials for the year ended 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 5.0% to 5.75%, increasing the cost of hire purchase and other borrowing. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 7.2% from $12.80 to $13.72 an hour from April 2026, lifting wage bills. (3) Wholesale recycled-paper and energy input costs have risen 13.5% year-on-year, while construction inflation is 7.1% and demand for insulation grew 4.2%.

questions.question_text: VIML is funding its $450,000 insulation line with $180,000 of hire purchase. Explain two advantages of hire purchase for VIML compared with paying the full $450,000 immediately from retained profit.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Hire purchase spreads the $180,000 cost over the life of the asset, so VIML keeps $270,000 of retained profit available as working capital against fixed costs of $240,000 a year and the 13.5% rise in recycled-paper and energy costs. The equipment is used while it is paid for, helping output of 80,000 units continue during the skills-gap problem.

Point 2: Hire purchase preserves cash for the $540-per-employee training needed to close the skills gap among 11 of 28 staff. Although the total cost is higher than paying cash, the line can start generating the $6.00 contribution per unit immediately, so investment and training proceed together without exhausting reserves.

Spreading payments also matches the benefits: the line starts producing contribution immediately (the $15.00 price less $9.00 variable cost gives $6.00 a roll), so cash generated helps meet instalments. Keeping $270,000 retained profit intact gives a buffer against 5.5% waste and 13.5% input inflation while the skills gap is closed.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage of hire purchase over using retained profit (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation applied to VIML's funding, costs and training needs.

questions.question_text: VIML wants to grow demand for recycled-fibre insulation. Consider advertising in building trade journals, running influencer campaigns on home-renovation social media, or sponsoring an eco-building exhibition. Which should VIML choose? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Trade journal advertising: Print adverts can explain the technical benefits of recycled-fibre insulation to the 300 builders surveyed and have a long reading life, but response is slow and hard to track. A campaign is costly for a firm committing $180,000 to hire purchase, and it cannot show the carbon data that 58% of builders say influences purchase as vividly as digital media.

Influencer campaigns on social media: Renovation influencers can demonstrate the product and publish supplier carbon data directly to the 58% of survey respondents who check it, at low cost per contact and with measurable engagement. The 66% who would switch if the price is within $0.30 can be targeted with a clear value message. Reach among traditional builders may be weaker, and results require sustained content, but campaigns can be scaled as the 80,000-unit line ramps up.

Eco-building exhibition sponsorship: A show stand allows face-to-face demonstrations and immediate contacts with specifiers, supporting the 58% carbon-data finding. Stand costs and staff time are high, however, and one event cannot sustain year-round orders for a 28-employee firm with a skills gap and a $240,000 fixed-cost base.

Recommendation: VIML should choose influencer campaigns on renovation social media, backed by simple carbon-data sheets for builders. They reach the price-sensitive 66% and carbon-aware 58% of the survey at controllable cost and can be measured against trial sales of 16,000 rolls. Trade journals are rejected as slow and untargeted; exhibitions are rejected because a single stand is expensive relative to the $450,000 line and cannot maintain steady demand.

level_1_1_to_4: Limited awareness of the three promotional options with minimal VIML context.
level_2_5_to_8: Discussion of advantages and disadvantages of at least two options applied to VIML's survey and costs.
level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three options with a justified recommendation explaining why journals and exhibitions are rejected.

questions.question_text: VIML has a skills gap in operating the new fibre line. Explain two benefits for VIML of its democratic leadership style.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Democratic leadership invites the 28 staff, including the 11 still needing on-the-job training, to share ideas on running the fibre line, so practical solutions to the skills gap come from the operators themselves. Involvement satisfies esteem needs (Maslow), raising commitment and helping reduce the 5.5% production waste and 2.7% defect rate.

Point 2: Regular discussion fits VIML's hierarchical structure by feeding front-line suggestions upward to Aisha Rahman without authoritarian instructions, so training at $540 per employee can be targeted at the real problems. Greater ownership supports retention and protects the 80,000-unit output while the $180,000 hire-purchase line beds in and the $6.00 contribution is established.

Involving operators also makes the $540 courses more effective, because staff can identify which machine settings cause the 2.7% defects. Better communication fits the hierarchical structure by passing practical ideas up to Aisha Rahman, supporting the 58% of builders who value supplier carbon data and helping the $180,000 line reach its 80,000-unit potential.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit of democratic leadership (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual development linked to VIML's skills gap, waste and costs.

questions.question_text: A training audit shows 11 of 28 VIML staff have not completed on-the-job training on the new fibre line. Consider on-the-job training or off-the-job courses at the college. Which should VIML choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
On-the-job training: Coaching at the fibre line teaches the exact machine settings VIML uses, costs no course fees and keeps all 11 untrained staff producing rolls, protecting the 16,000-roll trial sales and the drive to cut the 2.7% defect rate and 5.5% waste. Trainers' own output may fall and bad habits can spread, and there is no external certificate for builders who value carbon data, but the training is immediate and specific.

Off-the-job courses: The college course at $540 each would cost $5,940 for the 11 staff (11 x $540), affordable beside a $450,000 investment, and would give structured, certified skills that support the 58% of builders who check supplier data. It removes 11 of 28 workers from production temporarily and generic content may not match VIML's machines, so follow-up coaching is still needed.

Decision: VIML should choose on-the-job training first, adding short college certification for senior operators once the line is stable. It is cheaper, machine-specific and avoids losing output while the skills gap persists and $6.00 contribution per unit must cover $240,000 fixed costs. Full off-the-job training is rejected because taking 11 of 28 staff away from the line would disrupt the 80,000-unit target and its generic content would not directly reduce the 5.5% production waste.

Keeping training on site also protects VIML's specific recycled-fibre process knowledge, which a generic college course cannot teach. Management can track the 2.7% defect rate and 5.5% waste over the next quarter and add certified modules only where builders ask for evidence of supplier standards.

level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two training methods with limited VIML application.
level_2_5_to_8: Analysis of benefits and drawbacks of both methods using VIML's audit figures and costs.
level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both methods with a justified decision covering cost, disruption and machine relevance.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how VIML's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $240,000 ÷ ($15.00 − $9.00) = $240,000 ÷ $6.00 = 40,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 40,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $15.00 − $9.00 = $6.00. Answer: contribution per unit is $6.00.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways the management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Compare break-even of 40,000 units with output of 80,000 units, giving a margin of safety of 40,000 units, so VIML can judge how far trial sales of 16,000 rolls must grow before the line is secure.
2. Use the $6.00 contribution to test the survey finding that 66% would switch if price was within $0.30 of standard rolls: a $0.30 cut would still leave $5.70 contribution, so management can decide whether to price into that window.
3. Link the 40,000-unit break-even point to the $180,000 hire-purchase commitment, checking that contribution covers fixed costs and instalments before expanding into the 4.2%-growth insulation market.
4. Monitor average total cost of $12.00 a unit ($240,000 ÷ 80,000 = $3.00 plus $9.00) against 5.5% production waste and 13.5% input inflation, so managers can target the skills gap with $540 training where it protects margin most.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 40,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $6.00 | (iii) Four contextual uses explained: margin of safety of 40,000 units against 80,000 output; pricing within the $0.30 survey window on $6.00 contribution; hire-purchase affordability for the $180,000 commitment; and average total cost benchmarking at $12.00 to target 5.5% waste and 13.5% inflation.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula and 1 mark for the numerical answer in (i) and (ii); 1 mark per valid applied use in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate VIML's financial position by calculating the gross profit margin, profit margin and return on capital employed for 2024 and 2025. Has VIML's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Gross Profit Margin 2024 = 40.0%
Gross Profit Margin 2025 = 42.0%
Profit Margin 2024 = 16.0%
Profit Margin 2025 = 15.0%
ROCE 2024 = 18.0%
ROCE 2025 = 12.0%

Detailed workings: Gross profit of 720 on revenue of 1,800 gives 40.0% in 2024, and 840 on 2,000 gives 42.0% in 2025. Operating profit of 288 on revenue of 1,800 gives 16.0%, and 300 on 2,000 gives 15.0%. Operating profit of 288 on capital employed of 1,600 gives 18.0%, and 300 on 2,500 gives 12.0%. Revenue rose by 200 while cost of sales rose by 80, and interest payable rose from 30 to 45.

Evaluation: The picture is mixed rather than a clear improvement. The 40.0% to 42.0% gross margin shows better control of direct materials, despite 13.5% input inflation and 5.5% production waste. However the 16.0% to 15.0% operating margin fell because operating profit rose only 12 while revenue rose 200, so overheads and the skills-gap costs grew faster than sales. Most telling, the 18.0% to 12.0% return on capital employed fell sharply because capital employed jumped from 1,600 to 2,500 with the $450,000 insulation line while operating profit barely increased; interest payable also rose from 30 to 45 with the $180,000 hire-purchase commitment.

Conclusion: VIML's financial position has not improved overall. Only the gross margin rose; the operating margin slipped and ROCE fell markedly, showing the new $450,000 line is not yet earning a return on the extra capital. Management should focus on raising productivity, closing the skills gap and cutting 5.5% waste so that operating profit catches up with the enlarged capital base before further investment.

level_1_1_to_4: States isolated figures from Appendix 2 without accurate calculation.
level_2_5_to_8: Calculates all three measures for both years accurately and describes the mixed trend with some VIML context.
level_3_9_to_12: Accurate calculations for both years with detailed evaluation of revenue, costs, capital and interest, and a justified conclusion that overall position has not improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for VIML of using recycled-fibre insulation.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: Recycled fibre supports the 66% of 300 surveyed builders who would switch if the price was within $0.30 and the 58% who use supplier carbon data, protecting the $15.00 price and $6.00 contribution while recycled-paper and energy costs rise 13.5%. It also positions VIML for the 4.2% growth in insulation demand and the $450,000 line.

Disadvantage: Recycled fibre can settle unevenly and vary in quality, which may worsen the 2.7% defect rate and the 5.5% production waste, raising costs above the $9.00 variable cost. With 11 of 28 staff still untrained and $540 training costs, meeting the 80,000-unit output at consistent quality is difficult; if the $0.30 price window is not accepted, margin is squeezed just as hire-purchase payments begin.

VIML should therefore confirm that the 66% stated switching intention becomes paid trial orders before scaling the $450,000 line, and monitor whether the $0.30 price window can be met without eroding the $6.00 contribution.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual development using VIML's survey, costs and waste data.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 5.75%, the 7.2% minimum wage increase and the 13.5% rise in recycled-paper and energy input costs will affect VIML. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (5.0% to 5.75%): Hire purchase is the relevant borrowing. If the $180,000 commitment is variable-rate, a 0.75% rise adds 0.0075 x $180,000 = $1,350 a year; if fixed, there is no immediate change. This is modest beside $240,000 fixed costs, but VIML's Appendix 2 shows interest payable already rising from 30 to 45, so further increases would add pressure on a firm whose ROCE has fallen to 12.0%.

Minimum wage increase (7.2%, to $13.72 an hour): With a workforce of 28, wage costs rise in a business facing a skills gap. The insert gives no hours worked or individual pay, so an annual wage total cannot be stated. The defensible test is productivity: 80,000 units divided by 28 workers is about 2,857 rolls per worker, so the rise is affordable only if productivity holds or improves; otherwise unit labour cost rises and the $6.00 contribution shrinks, aggravating the fall in operating margin to 15.0%.

Recycled-paper and energy costs (13.5%): An illustrative upper bound is that the whole $9.00 variable cost rises 13.5%, adding $1.22 a unit (0.135 x $9.00 = $1.215), which at 80,000 units is about $97,200 a year (80,000 x $1.215). Even partial pass-through would cut the $6.00 contribution heavily. The $0.30 price window and carbon-data preference may recover some of this, but 13.5% is larger than any offset available.

Conclusion: The 13.5% rise in recycled-paper and energy input costs has the greatest impact. It compounds across all 80,000 units and directly reduces the $6.00 contribution needed to cover hire-purchase payments and reverse the fall in ROCE, whereas the interest effect is about $1,350 and the wage effect can be managed through productivity. VIML should prioritise waste reduction and input-cost negotiation.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited identification of the external factors with minimal application to VIML.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analysis of the impact of at least two of the three changes on VIML's costs, revenue or financing.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three changes in context with a well-justified greatest-impact judgement.
